intro: Introduction to European Union Law. Lecture one: introduction and basics — what the Union is, how it came to be, and the map of everything this half of the course covers.

slides.7: One fact worth keeping from the opening: the President of the European Council is António Costa of Portugal, in office since December 2024. And do not confuse the three presidencies — the European Council, the Commission, and the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.
slides.10: The whole course in one diagram. It returns at the start of every lecture, and it is worth learning as the skeleton of the European half of the exam. It has five parts, so build them in order. First, the institutions under Article 13, paragraph 1 of the Treaty on European Union: the European Council, the Commission, the Council of the European Union, the Parliament, and the Court of Justice with its five procedures — preliminary references, annulment, failure to act, infringement, and others — plus other institutions and non-institutional actors. Second, competences and procedures: competences are exclusive, shared or complementary; procedures are ordinary, special, and trilogues. Third, the sources, arranged as a hierarchy running downwards: primary law — the two Treaties, the Charter, the protocols and general principles; then secondary law — regulations, directives and decisions; then tertiary law — delegated and implementing acts; then soft law; and finally the role of member state law. Fourth, the unique features that make the Union supranational: primacy; enforcement, which is direct and decentralised, with procedural autonomy, effectiveness and equivalence; direct effect, with its conditions and the vertical–horizontal distinction; indirect effect; and state and tortious liability. And fifth, fundamental rights, together with the basics of internal market and competition law.
slides.15: How the course runs. Classes are in person, live-streamed via Zoom without video — slides and audio only — and recorded and made available the same way. The recordings are offered with the October 2026 exam in view, which is the sitting you are preparing for. The lecturer also states plainly that in-person participation correlates with a higher success rate.
slides.32: The course map returns — the same five-part overview as at the start, and it comes back throughout the course with the current topic marked. If you can rebuild those five parts from memory, you have the shape of the whole exam.
slides.38: Enlargement, as a timeline. Six member states in 1957 — Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. Nine in 1973, with Denmark, Ireland and the United Kingdom. Ten in 1981, with Greece. Twelve in 1986, with Portugal and Spain. Fifteen in 1995, with Austria, Finland and Sweden. Twenty-five in 2004 — Cyprus, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia. Twenty-seven in 2007, with Bulgaria and Romania. Twenty-eight in 2013, with Croatia. And back to twenty-seven in 2020, when the United Kingdom left. The current candidates are Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia, Albania, North Macedonia and Kosovo — and Turkey, a candidate with no active accession talks.
